method: Rebuild from primary text. Cal. Lab. Code §925 and Cal. Civ. Code §§1646 and 1646.5 were fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read in full. LGCY Power v. Superior Court was read on CourtListener directly rather than relied on through the ea_ca_925 finding, and it quotes §925 in full. This clause carried the same 'primarily works in California' defect already confirmed in ea_ca_925, which is what a propagated error looks like. Assertions describe the REBUILT body.

assertions.text: parties to a contract relating to a transaction involving in the aggregate not less than $250,000 may agree that California law governs, whether or not the transaction bears a reasonable relation to this state
assertions.note: Civ. Code §1646.5, verbatim. The previous body said 'a contract of at least a quarter million dollars', which reads as the contract price; the section says a transaction 'involving in the aggregate' that amount.

assertions.text: §1646.5 validates a choice of California law and does not apply to a contract for labor or personal services, to a transaction primarily for personal, family or household purposes, or to the extent Commercial Code §1301(c) provides otherwise
assertions.note: Civ. Code §1646.5, second sentence. The labor and personal-services exclusion is the one that matters for this clause, because the clause is about individuals performing services. The previous body cited §1646.5 and stated none of its exclusions.

assertions.text: §925 covers an employee who primarily resides AND works in California
assertions.note: §925(a), quoted in full by the Court of Appeal in LGCY Power. The previous body said 'who primarily works in California', which covers people the section does not. This is the same defect confirmed in ea_ca_925 and it had propagated here.

assertions.text: the prohibition attaches to requiring the provision as a condition of employment, and adjudication includes arbitration
the provision is voidable at the employee's election, not void, and voiding it produces a California forum under California law
assertions.note: §925(b). LGCY quotes the San Diego Superior Court on the point: 'The language here is permissive: providing only that certain contractual provisions are voidable', and notes there was no evidence the parties had exercised the option. A commercial party reading only that a provision is 'voidable' may not realise nothing happens until the employee acts.

assertions.text: §925 applies only to a contract entered into, modified or extended on or after January 1, 2017
assertions.note: §925(f). Absent from the previous body. LGCY is a working illustration of why it matters: the defendants there signed before 2017 and argued their agreements were modified afterwards on promotion, and the trial court accepted an oral modification after that date as enough at the demurrer stage.

assertions.text: §925 does not apply where the employee was in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the venue, forum or choice-of-law term
assertions.note: §925(e). Absent from the previous body, and it is the one lawful route to a non-California forum, so omitting it told the reader the door was shut when the statute leaves it open.

priorDefects: contradicted: 'any employee ... who primarily works in California'. §925(a) reads 'primarily resides and works'. Propagated from ea_ca_925.
unsupported: 'and, in practice, of any misclassified contractor'. Nothing read here supports extending §925 to contractors. The rebuilt body states the question instead of answering it.
omitted: that the provision is voidable at the employee's election rather than void.
omitted: every exclusion in Civ. Code §1646.5, including the labor and personal-services exclusion, which is the one that bears on this clause's subject.
imprecise: §1646.5 permits choosing California law. The clause presented it as general support for 'a governing law clause is generally enforceable'.
gaps: Whether §925 reaches a worker engaged as an independent contractor and later reclassified as an employee was not resolved. The clause now names the question. LGCY records that the employer there argued the California defendants were contractors and not employees; the opinion did not decide it.

Federal Arbitration Act preemption of §925 where the covered provision is an arbitration clause was not researched. For a commercial agreement that arbitrates, that is the question on which the clause's practical value turns.

Nothing read here validates a choice of another state's law in a California-connected commercial contract. §1646.5 permits choosing California law and §1646 supplies the default. The clause states the limit of what was verified and does not answer the more common drafting question.
Code of Civil Procedure §410.40, the forum-selection counterpart to §1646.5, was not read.

judicialQuotations.case: LGCY Power, LLC v. Superior Court (Cal. Ct. App. 2022)
judicialQuotations.quote: California Labor Code section 925 went into effect on January 1, 2017, and provides that employers cannot force an employee who resides and works primarily in California to agree, as a condition of employment, to: (1) litigate a claim arising in California in a forum outside of California; or (2) waive the employee's right to the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California.

judicialQuotations.quote: (a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. judicialQuotations.quote: The language here is permissive: providing only that certain contractual provisions are "voidable"

singleOpinionCaveat: LGCY Power's holding is that §925 supplies an exception to the compulsory cross-complaint statute — a question of first impression. It is used here for its recitation of §925, which matches leginfo word for word, and for the voidable-not-void point it takes from another court's order. The rebuild rests on the statutory text. The second quotation above is truncated in the source excerpt at 'the substant...' and should be re-read in full before it is quoted where a reader will rely on it.
